title: Internationalizing IPv6 Using 128-Bit Unicode
summary: This is an April 1st humor RFC. It jokes that Unicode will run out of code points and that the next size will be 128 bits, then suggests ways to link that to IPv6 addresses. It should not be read as a real proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a joke paper that imagines letters getting so big that each one is as long as a computer address. It is for a smile.

subtitle: Using 128-bit Unicode code points for IPv6 addresses

tldr.problem: Unicode will eventually exhaust its current 1.1 million code points due to exponential growth in emojis and custom characters. A larger code point space is needed, and it could conveniently be 128 bits like IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st RFC proposes that 128-bit Unicode code points be created and then used for IPv6 addresses, allowing addresses to be represented as emoji glyphs and enabling multicast groups for any character (like `:cat:` for cat content).
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st humor document. While technically creative, it is not a real proposal and should not be implemented. It jokes that solving IPv6 adoption and Unicode exhaustion together would require decades of standardization work.

today: RFC 8369 is an April 1st humor document published in the Independent Submission stream. It should not be treated as a real proposal. While humorous, it reflects real observations: Unicode is indeed growing exponentially, IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, and standardization is time-consuming. The document plays with these facts to create an absurdist vision.

sections.title: The Problem Setup
sections.content:
This is an April 1st humor RFC that combines two imaginative premises: that Unicode will eventually exhaust its current code point space due to emoji growth, and that the solution would be 128-bit Unicode code points that could be leveraged for IPv6.

The RFC notes that Unicode currently supports 1.1 million code points (formally a limit of UTF-16), with 136,755 already allocated. More are added yearly for new scripts, symbols, and emojis, while none are removed. The argument is that at exponential growth rates, the space will eventually fill.

The document then jokes that expanding Unicode to 128 bits would 'keep the IETF busy for decades,' enable new market opportunities, increase tax revenues, and ultimately reduce global warming.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone wrote a joke paper saying emoji symbols are taking up all the space in the Unicode system, and IPv6 addresses could solve it by being 128 bits, just like code points would be.

sections.title: The Proposal
sections.content:
The RFC proposes representing IPv6 addresses as Unicode code points, with several humorous implications: addresses could be typed as emoji glyphs instead of hex (e.g., a computer could be named ':cat:'), network monitoring tools would display pretty glyphs instead of address strings, and older hex notation could be deprecated in favor of Unicode syntax like 'U+20010DB885A3000000008A2E03707334'.

The RFC defines new terms like imoji (individual-specific emoji, like one for each human), amoji (alien emoji, if we meet extraterrestrials), and omoji (obfuscated identity emoji for privacy).

Multicast groups would use the high-order bit of the 128-bit code point space: `:cat:` would be a general cat multicast group, while `:garfield:` would be the specific Garfield cat multicast group. The RFC even jokes about Martian addresses being 'Bogons' and future Martian addresses being 'Bigons,' playing on the word 'bygones.'
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of typing computer addresses as numbers, you would use emoji symbols. All cat content could have one address, and Garfield could have his own address.

sections.title: The Absurdity
sections.content:
The document humously notes that routing would have 'some exponential growth' due to difficulties in aggregating code points, but this would be 'offset by increases in processor and memory capacity' and drive 'the need to frequently upgrade networking hardware,' boosting the global economy and reducing global warming.

A special case is mentioned: RFC 8136's UFO (User Security Flag Option) for IPv6 is cited as supporting a scenario where alien species need their own code points. The document suggests that 'scenic routing' (RFC 7511, another April Fools RFC) could specify which exact scenery to visit, and that avian carriers (RFC 1149) could be used for transport, though they only support IPv4.

The ultimate joke is that while all this is humorous, it highlights real technical challenges: Unicode is indeed growing, IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, and IETF standardization takes a long time.
sections.plainLanguage: The funny paper imagines routers getting bigger and computers upgrading more often, which somehow helps the environment. It also jokes about aliens and pigeons delivering packets.
